extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in Operation Car Wash / Brazilian corruption investigations
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic (Wikipedia-style) article describing the Operation Car Wash (Operação Lava Jato) corruption investigation in Brazil, including legal procedures, leaked materials, implicated companies and people, and related judicial and political developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delação premiada (rewarded collaboration / plea bargain)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Colaboração premiada – literally, 'rewarded collaboration'; the common name for the legal process known as delação premiada. Delação premiada – 'rewarded whistleblowing' (or, 'informing'). A legal process by which a suspect is offered a specific reduced sentence prescribed by law, in return for turning in accomplices, or aiding in investigations. The common name for it in Brazil is Colaboração premiada ('rewarded collaboration'). The concept is similar to a plea bargain, in return for investigative assistance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout Operation Car Wash as a procedural tool: suspects may obtain reduced sentences by providing information about accomplices and corrupt schemes. The entry explains the term and parallels to plea bargains, implying that descriptions of investigations should clarify the legal basis, limits, and effects of such agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic verification and collaborative vetting of leaked materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The Intercept Brasil published leaked Telegram chat messages; other news agencies such as Folha de São Paulo and Veja "confirmed the authenticity of the messages and worked in partnership with The Intercept Brasil to sort the rest of the material in their possession before releasing it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting on leaked/confidential material, the article highlights the practice of cross-outlet verification and coordination prior to publication. Good practice: confirm authenticity with independent outlets, sort and redact materials carefully, and document verification steps. The Intercept's collaboration with other media is given as an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press freedom protections under the 1988 Brazilian Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Intercept "cited provisions for freedom of the press in the 1988 Brazilian Constitution." Supreme Court justice Gilmar Mendes "ruled that any investigation of Greenwald in connection with the reporting would be illegal under the Brazilian constitution, calling freedom of the press a 'pillar of democracy'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting and judicial actions involving journalists are constrained by constitutionally protected press freedoms. The page treats press freedom as a legal shield against certain investigative actions by the state; writers should reference constitutional protections when describing state responses to journalistic leaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on improper collaboration between judges and prosecutors
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaked conversations (Vaza Jato) accused then-judge Sergio Moro and lead prosecutor Deltan Dallagnol of "violating legal procedure during the investigation, trial and arrest of former president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva," with allegations that prosecutors and judges colluded to influence outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key evaluative standard for the conduct of investigations and prosecutions is adherence to impartial legal procedure and separation between prosecutors and the judiciary. The article treats collusion between actors (judge/prosecutor coordination) as misconduct that undermines the legitimacy of prosecutions and may lead to annulment of convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal limits and requirements for international cooperation in investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: In March 2020 the Intercept reported that Brazilian prosecutors had secretly collaborated with the US Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation in a manner "that may have violated international legal treaties and Brazilian law." The Brazilian Ministry of Justice had not been informed; making this collaboration illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-border investigative cooperation must comply with international treaties and domestic legal procedures (including informing appropriate ministries). Secret or unauthorized cooperation can be characterized as potentially illegal and can be a basis for criticism or judicial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and oversight of corporate leniency/settlement agreements in corruption cases
rubrics_metrics.description: References to Odebrecht's leniency/plea arrangements and companies recognizing cartel behaviour: e.g., "Em acordo com Cade, empreiteiras reconhecem cartel na 'lava jato'" and mentions of leniency/settlement commitments being approved by the competition authority (Cade).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate leniency agreements and admissions of cartel conduct are instruments used to resolve corporate involvement in corruption; such agreements typically involve recognition of wrongdoing and commitments approved by relevant authorities (e.g., competition authority). Descriptions should note the role of oversight agencies and the legal/administrative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutionality requirement for special prosecutorial funds and initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecutors proposed using money paid by companies in the US to set up an "independent fund to fight corruption." "This attempt was then deemed unconstitutional by Brazil's Supreme Court."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutorial initiatives that create special funds or channels for seized/collected money must comply with constitutional rules; the Supreme Court can void such measures if they lack constitutional basis. Coverage should flag constitutionality as a key test of such measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolving jurisprudence regarding imprisonment after appeals (second-instance detention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article documents judicial developments: e.g., "STF ratifica regra para prisão defendida pela Operação Lava Jato" and later references that the Supreme Court "volta a proibir prisão em 2ª instância; placar foi 6 a 5."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules on when convicted defendants may be imprisoned (after conviction in second instance or only after all appeals) are substantive legal standards that can materially affect high-profile cases. The entry treats shifts in Supreme Court precedent as central to understanding outcomes and legal legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and ethical considerations around use of hacked/leaked materials as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaked Telegram chats were obtained after a hacker (Walter Delgatti Neto) broke into authorities' Telegram accounts by abusing Telegram's phone number verification and exploiting voicemail vulnerabilities; the Intercept neither confirmed nor denied the source and relied on press freedom protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provenance of leaked or hacked materials raises legal and ethical questions: investigators, courts, and journalists must consider whether acquisition methods violated laws or procedures and how that affects admissibility or public-interest defenses. The article highlights the tension between press freedom and potential illegality of source actions.
